factors.factor: Untested code path: the new Service Control quota-policy code was never exercised during the region-by-region rollout because it only activates when a policy change triggers it, so the null-pointer bug went undetected before reaching production.
factors.evidence: "This code change and binary release went through a region by region rollout, but the new code path was never exercised during this rollout because it needed a policy change to trigger it."

factors.factor: Insufficient input validation: the new code path did not handle blank fields in policy data, causing a null pointer crash when the malformed policy was read.
factors.evidence: "This pulled in blank fields for this policy change and exercised the new code path, which hit a null pointer and caused the binaries to go into a crash loop."

factors.factor: Unsafe global replication of configuration data: a policy change with unintended blank fields was replicated globally within seconds without a staged or validated rollout, so the bad data reached every region at once.
factors.evidence: "This metadata was replicated globally within seconds. This policy data contained unintended blank fields."

factors.factor: Global simultaneous impact: the crash loop occurred in every regional deployment at once, turning a single bad config into a worldwide outage rather than a contained regional one.
factors.evidence: "This occurred globally, in each regional deployment."

factors.factor: Slow mitigation due to the red-button kill switch requiring a rollout to take effect: despite fast detection, recovery waited on deploying the disable mechanism across regions.
factors.evidence: "The red-button was ready to roll out, ~25 minutes from the start of the incident." and "Within 40 minutes of the incident, the red-button rollout was completed, and recovery started across regions"

factors.factor: Thundering herd on recovery: restarting Service Control tasks simultaneously overloaded the underlying Spanner table in large regions, prolonging recovery in us-central1 to roughly 2h 40m.
factors.evidence: "as Service Control tasks restarted, it created a herd effect on the underlying infrastructure it depends on (the Spanner table), overloading that infrastructure."

factors.factor: Lack of restart/backoff safeguards and load control during recovery, requiring manual throttling and traffic rerouting by the team.
factors.evidence: "The team throttled task creation to minimize the impact on the underlying infrastructure and routed traffic to multi-regional databases to reduce the load."

factors.factor: Shared dependency on Google Cloud for status communication: the status page infrastructure ran on the affected platform, delaying the first customer-facing report.
factors.evidence: "The first incident report was posted to Cloud Service Health ~1h after the start of the crashes, because the Cloud Service Health infrastructure was down due to this outage."

factors.factor: Customer monitoring dependency on affected infrastructure: customers' monitoring running on Google Cloud also failed, leaving them without incident signal.
factors.evidence: "For some customers, the monitoring infrastructure they had running on Google Cloud was also failing, leaving them without a signal of the incident or an understanding of the impact."

factors.factor: Absence of a workaround for customers during the outage, limiting customer-side mitigation options.
